parts.note: a breaker-in of fillies would be a 'filly buster'; said together that sounds like the word for a speaker who talks on and on to block a vote

explanation.surface: A horse-breaker who never stops talking while taming young mares.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'buster' breaks in horses and a 'filly' is a young mare; run the two together and you hear the parliamentary term for obstructing by endless speeches.
explanation.definitionFit: A parliamentary obstructionist who delays a vote with interminable speeches is long-winded by design.

definitions.meaning: the ancient Roman marketplace and public square
a place or meeting for public discussion

explanation.surface: A place in Rome where trade and discussion went on.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman public square served as marketplace, and the word now means any place for open discussion.

indicators.note: an ocean dial that registers readings is shown with its letters set out anew, read here as rearranging them

explanation.surface: A nautical dial is reading 'lukewarm' for the local water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'registers' rearranges OCEAN DIAL. In Revelation the church at Laodicea is 'neither cold nor hot', so the place's people stand for half-heartedness.
explanation.definitionFit: The Laodicean church was rebuked in Revelation for being half-hearted, so its citizens' name means indifferent in faith.

parts.note: plumed suggests the feathered serpent god, but a feather stole shares its name with a large crushing snake

explanation.surface: The feathered serpent god of the Aztecs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Plumed Serpent' is Quetzalcoatl (and a Lawrence novel); a feathered boa is a scarf, and the big snake shares its first word.
explanation.definitionFit: A large snake that kills by squeezing, whose first word is also a feathered scarf.

parts.note: reads as choosing the correct path, but the right-hand lane is where fast traffic overtakes on British roads

explanation.surface: A driver chose the correct route.
explanation.walkthrough: On British roads, which drive on the left, the right-hand lane is the overtaking or fast lane.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving into the fast lane means going more quickly, i.e. driving at high velocity.

parts.note: a small pointed tuft on the chin is called an imperial, after Napoleon III, so its wearer is peculiarly the ruler

explanation.surface: A question about a man with an odd beard.
explanation.walkthrough: An 'imperial' is a small pointed chin beard named after Napoleon III; the clue asks who is 'peculiarly' (in his own special way) bearded, the man with the imperial.
explanation.definitionFit: The ruler of an empire gives his title's adjective to a pointed chin beard, the imperial.

clue.text: With fire it cooked many a goose in war and peace

definitions.text: With fire it cooked many a goose in war and peace

parts.words: With fire it cooked many a goose in war and peace
parts.note: add 'fire' and you get the wartime fighter plane that cooked the enemy's goose; alone it is the roasting rod that cooks a goose in peacetime

explanation.surface: A nod to Tolstoy's novel, as if a goose were roasted through war and peace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'War and Peace' looks like the novel, but it means wartime and peacetime: the Spitfire aircraft in war, the kitchen roasting rod in peace. 'Cooked his goose' means ruined him.
explanation.definitionFit: A roasting rod turned over a fire cooks meat such as goose, and with 'fire' added it names the famous RAF fighter plane.

clue.text: Hot taps out of order-we're gravelled!

indicators.note: out of order says the letters are not in their proper sequence and must be rearranged

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot on a tap

explanation.surface: Broken hot taps leave a householder stumped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gravelled' also means baffled, but here it is garden walks covered in gravel. 'out of order' rearranges H and TAPS.
explanation.definitionFit: Garden walks and tracks are often surfaced with gravel.

clue.text: " Is there anybody there ? " he said

definitions.text: " Is there anybody there ? " he said

parts.words: " Is there anybody there ? " he said
parts.note: the opening words of Walter de la Mare's poem The Listeners, spoken by a man knocking at a moonlit door

explanation.surface: Someone calls into an empty house.
explanation.walkthrough: De la Mare's poem begins: '"Is there anybody there?" said the Traveller, / Knocking on the moonlit door.'
explanation.definitionFit: In the poem the speaker is a wayfarer on horseback who knocks at a lonely house.

clue.text: Where you are at breakfast time, if you don't want to be this

definitions.text: Where you are at breakfast time, if you don't want to be this

parts.words: Where you are at breakfast time, if you don't want to be this
parts.note: a reader at breakfast is hidden behind the newspaper of that name, and reading it keeps you from being out of date

explanation.surface: Advice to read the paper at breakfast to keep up with events.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means old-fashioned; at breakfast a reader of The Times sits behind it, so reading the paper keeps you up to date.
explanation.definitionFit: Being old-fashioned or out of date with current events, which reading the morning paper prevents.

annotationWithheld.why: 'What's up in housebuilding ? (7)' as held gives no parse to ROOTAGE (a root system); no reversal or pun links the clue words to the answer as printed

clue.text: Their pluck is not without strain

definitions.text: Their pluck is not without strain

parts.words: Their pluck is not without strain
parts.note: pluck reads as courage and strain as stress, but these small picks pluck strings and a strain is a tune

explanation.surface: Brave folk whose courage costs them some stress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pluck' and 'strain' suggest nerve under pressure; musically, the picks pluck guitar or lute strings and so produce a strain, a melody.
explanation.definitionFit: The small picks used to pluck the strings of a guitar or lute produce music, a strain.

parts.note: an indent is an order for goods, made by correspondence; battledress hints at chain armour, which shares its name with the post

explanation.surface: A soldier puts in a requisition for a new battledress uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: An 'indent' is an official order for supplies; 'correspondingly' means by post, and old battledress was chain armour, which is called mail, so it is ordering mail by mail.
explanation.definitionFit: Buying goods through the post is purchasing by correspondence, and chain armour was the knight's battledress.

definitions.meaning: to utter is to put out or emit, as a statement is given out
kids are offspring, a family's descendants

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry about thoroughly dreadful children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Utter' looks like an adjective meaning complete, but it is the verb meaning to put out.
explanation.definitionFit: To give out a statement is to utter it, and children are a parent's offspring, both senses of the same word.

clue.text: He was between laughter and tears at the royal command

definitions.text: He was between laughter and tears at the royal command

parts.words: He was between laughter and tears at the royal command
parts.note: in the Scottish ballad, a knight laughs at the first line of the king's letter ordering him to sea and weeps at the next

explanation.surface: A courtier torn between laughing and crying at the king's order.
explanation.walkthrough: The old ballad of Sir Patrick Spens: the king sends him to sail in winter; reading the letter, he laughs, then tears blind him, and he drowns on the voyage.
explanation.definitionFit: The ballad's captain, ordered to sea by the king of Scotland, first laughed and then wept at the royal letter.

indicators.note: devoted in its old sense of given over or consigned, so the letters are handed over to a new order

explanation.surface: A call to fathers to rise, or a tribute to devoted mothers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'devoted' rearranges UP SIRES OR. The heads of convents are each called Mother Superior, so mothers in that sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Heads of convents are each addressed as Mother Superior, so religious mothers who rank above the nuns.

clue.text: Paradoxically he could show dread of what is bad

indicators.note: paradoxically suggests things turned contrary to expectation, so the letters of dread are put in a different order

parts.note: what is bad is evil

explanation.surface: A fearless man who, oddly, could be shown to fear wickedness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paradoxically' is the anagram signal; the paradox in the surface is that a fearless man could be said to show dread at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A reckless man who fears nothing is a person, so the pronoun stands for him.

parts.note: a natural in the card game is an ace and a ten-card dealt as the first two cards, totalling twenty-one

explanation.surface: A game that comes naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: In the French card game also called pontoon, a 'natural' is twenty-one with the first two cards, the best hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A card game aiming for a total of twenty-one, in which a two-card twenty-one is called a natural.

clue.text: The pagan spirit to tempt a fellow in charge of silver ?

parts.note: Pan was the Greek god of shepherds and woods, a pagan nature spirit
to tempt someone is to try them, as in testing
a fellow is a man

explanation.surface: A heathen spirit tempts a butler responsible for the family silver.
explanation.walkthrough: In a big house the man who looked after the pantry kept the silver and plate.
explanation.definitionFit: A servant who has charge of a household's pantry also looks after its silverware and plate.

parts.note: myosotis is the botanical name of the forget-me-not, whose name is itself a plea to be remembered

explanation.surface: A botanist names a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: Myosotis is the forget-me-not; by its very name ('namely') it is a keepsake that reminds.
explanation.definitionFit: A keepsake that reminds one of a person, as the forget-me-not's name asks to be remembered.

indicators.note: as here means in the guise of, so the letters of dons led are recast in another form

explanation.surface: University dons led the way as leaders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heads' looks like leaders, matching dons who led, but it means skulls; 'as' rearranges DONS LED.
explanation.definitionFit: Noddle is an old informal word for the head or skull.

parts.note: the old oath 'on my honour, bright' is turned into a girl's first name followed by a surname

explanation.surface: A clever young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Honour bright!' was a schoolchild's oath; the clue treats the first word as a girl's first name and 'Bright' as her surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's first name that, with 'Bright' after it, makes an old oath of sincerity.

clue.text: A single, just one, to reach a century — that's in character

parts.note: a single is one run in cricket
one is the Roman numeral I
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a century

explanation.surface: A batsman needs just one single to reach his hundred, which is typical of him.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture is apt: a single scores one run. Runes are the letters of the old Germanic alphabet, so this means written in those characters.
explanation.definitionFit: Runes were the characters of the ancient Germanic alphabet, so writing in them is being set down in those letters.

parts.note: a sleepyhead nods off, and the old word for a simpleton is built on nodding

explanation.surface: A drowsy person.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means a fool or simpleton, and also suggests someone who nods with sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for a fool, suggesting one who nods drowsily.

clue.text: Thinks comrades get split up by the turn of the tide

indicators.note: the word for comrades is split open so that another piece fits inside it

parts.note: comrades are mates

indicators.note: the turn of the tide means the word tide is read backwards

explanation.surface: A man ponders as his friends are separated by the tide turning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comrades' as MATES is a common crossword equivalence; 'the turn of' reverses the tide, and 'get split up by' opens MATES after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To ponder or reflect deeply is to engage in contemplation.

parts.note: Moor suggests Othello, but it is the Somerset moor of the 1685 battle, whose first part is a marsh grass

explanation.surface: Othello, the Moor, under attack.
explanation.walkthrough: Sedgemoor in Somerset was the site of the last battle on English soil (1685); the plant word joins 'moor' to name it.
explanation.definitionFit: A grass-like marsh plant whose name begins the Somerset moor where the Monmouth rebellion was crushed.

clue.text: " Methinks how slow This wanes ! " (M. N. Dream)

definitions.text: Methinks how slow This wanes ! " (M. N. Dream)

parts.words: Methinks how slow This wanes ! " (M. N. Dream)
parts.note: Theseus, waiting for his wedding in the opening lines of Shakespeare's comedy, complains of the waning month that delays it

explanation.surface: A line from A Midsummer Night's Dream with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: Theseus opens the play impatient for his wedding at the new moon: 'but, O, methinks, how slow this old moon wanes!'
explanation.definitionFit: The waning lunar phase before the new month is the end of the month's cycle, which Theseus wishes away.

clue.text: The liability of having little money in cover

indicators.note: in tells us one piece goes inside the word for cover

parts.note: a cover on a pot is a lid
a mite is a tiny coin, a very small sum

explanation.surface: A man who owes debts despite having only a little cash put aside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is the container signal. Limited liability means shareholders lose no more than their stake, as in 'Ltd'; the widow's mite is the Bible's tiny coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A company whose members' liability is restricted to their shares is described by that word, as in 'Ltd'.

parts.note: Terriers suggests the Territorial Army's part-time soldiers, but these are the dogs named after a Hebridean island

explanation.surface: A base abroad for the Territorial Army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terriers' was a nickname for Territorial Army soldiers; the clue means the long-haired terrier breed named after its Scottish island home.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish island in the Inner Hebrides gives its name to a breed of long-coated terrier.

clue.text: Intelligence sadly lacked by the Trojans

definitions.text: Intelligence sadly lacked by the Trojans

parts.words: Intelligence sadly lacked by the Trojans
parts.note: the Trojans dragged the Greeks' wooden horse inside their walls, showing no good sense about horses

explanation.surface: The defenders of Troy lacked the common sense that would have saved them.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means plain good sense; Troy fell because its people accepted the wooden horse, so they lacked sense about horses too.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain practical good judgment, the common sense the Trojans lacked when they took in the wooden horse.
